prompts.concept: Neighbor-Joining scores every pair by Q before it joins. On the earlier datasets the closest pair in the matrix was a tempting wrong pick — does NJ join the closest pair first here? Pick a cell in the matrix, or click two leaves.
prompts.math: NJ joins the pair minimizing Q(i,j) = (n-2)·d(i,j) - R_i - R_j. Each cluster's total distance to everything else counts, not just the pair's own distance.
prompts.reveal: This time the tempting pick is right: Escherichia_coli and Salmonella_enterica — two enteric bacteria — are the closest pair in the matrix AND NJ's first join (UPGMA opens with them too, under every model and gap treatment on this data). The closest pair does not always win — on the primate and globin data NJ's first join was elsewhere.

prompts.concept: The NJ run's last join: past it the finished tree is an unrooted NJ tree — on a UPGMA run this position is still mid-run, two of its 26 merges remain. Read the finished NJ tree by its splits: the two enteric bacteria together (Escherichia with Salmonella); the two mollicutes together (Mycoplasmoides with Spiroplasma); the two cyanobacteria together (Nostoc with Synechococcus); the Deinococcus–Thermus pair; a Bacillus–Staphylococcus firmicute pair; and an alphaproteobacterial triple (Agrobacterium, Caulobacter and Rickettsia).
prompts.math: Every internal edge of an unrooted tree defines a split; two trees are the same tree exactly when their split sets match. The bootstrap run next asks how many resampled trees rebuild each split.

prompts.concept: Each number on a branch is a count — of the resampled trees that rebuilt that grouping — never a probability that the grouping is true. MEGA's run drew its own resamples — its bootstrap has no seed — so its counts differ from yours wherever support is short of total, and a rerun of MEGA itself would differ again; the strong groupings agree either way. Now do the handout's step 6: switch the gap treatment to complete deletion and run again — which groupings keep their counts, and which move?

lab.title: MEGA: 100 bootstrap replicates on 16S rRNA
objectives: Run MEGA's NJ tree with a 100-replicate bootstrap test on a 27-taxon bacterial 16S rRNA alignment, under pairwise then complete deletion
Match each MEGA analysis option to the NeoPhylo control that reproduces it — including the seed MEGA does not offer
Read bootstrap support as a count of replicate trees, and compare two independent 100-replicate samples within sampling noise
lab.handout_md:
## What this lab reproduces

MEGA's bootstrap chain: a Neighbor-Joining tree on a Kimura 2-parameter distance matrix with the bootstrap test of phylogeny — every option set as the settings table lists it — run twice on a gapped 27-taxon alignment: under pairwise deletion (MEGA's default gap treatment) and under complete deletion, 100 replicates each. The numbers you reproduce are MEGA's own, recorded from MEGA-CC 12.1.4.

## The data

27 bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA sequences — one genus each, from Escherichia coli to Caulobacter — over 1,628 aligned sites, with real indels: pairwise deletion keeps all 1,628 columns available to each pair; complete deletion keeps the 1,199 columns where all 27 sequences carry a base. The sequences are NCBI RefSeq records aligned with MAFFT, bundled as the `16s-rrna` library dataset.

To cross-check in MEGA itself: load this lab, export the alignment as `.meg` from NeoPhylo's Export menu, open that file in MEGA, and apply the settings table exactly — the same NJ tree run twice, once per gap treatment.

## Before you start

Read the settings table. In MEGA the run's options live in the analysis dialog you reach from the menu path in the second column; the table lists every option the runs set — nothing is left to a default — next to the NeoPhylo control that reproduces it. One row has no MEGA counterpart: MEGA's bootstrap is unseeded, so two runs draw different resamples — NeoPhylo's Seed is what makes your run reproducible.

## Steps

1. Load this lab. NeoPhylo loads the alignment and computes the K80 matrix — MEGA's "Kimura 2-parameter" — under pairwise deletion.
2. Look at the matrix before the tree. Which pair looks closest? Write your prediction down — NJ does not always join the closest pair first.
3. Step through the joins (or jump to the end) and read the finished tree as unrooted: which bacterial groups does it recover?
4. Open the "How sure are we?" panel. Run the bootstrap with the table's settings — MEGA's Test of Phylogeny: Bootstrap method at 100 replicates. The numbers that land on the tree's internal branches are counts of replicate trees.
5. Switch the Gap treatment control to Complete deletion — the second MEGA run — build the tree again, then run the bootstrap again.
6. Compare the two runs: the trees' groupings first, then the support on each grouping.

## Questions

- A support value is a count — of the resampled trees that rebuilt that grouping — never a probability that the grouping is true. Which groupings sit at the top of your tally: the small pairs, or the deep groupings?
- MEGA's bootstrap is unseeded: a second MEGA run on the same file draws different resamples, so MEGA's own numbers move run to run too. MEGA's Tree Explorer draws the inferred NJ tree with support printed as a percent on each internal branch — 98 on a branch means 98 of the run's 100 replicate trees contained that grouping. Its Newick export writes the same supports as proportions to four decimals (`0.9800`), so the file puts 0.98 where the screen showed 98; NeoPhylo shows the percent on the branch and writes integer percents (`98`) in its Newick export.

MEGA's bootstrap has no seed: run the same file twice and the resamples differ, so MEGA's own support values move run to run — two of its 100-replicate runs are the handout's recorded values, one sample each. NeoPhylo's Seed makes your run reproducible — but it is its own sample, never MEGA's. Two independent 100-replicate samples agree only within sampling noise: expect the strong groupings to land alike and the middling ones to differ, just as a rerun of MEGA itself would differ. A support is the percent of replicates in which the split appeared — never a probability that the grouping is true.

Complete deletion changes which columns each replicate resamples: MEGA removes filtered sites before the analysis begins, so a kept-columns run and a full-columns run draw their resamples from different site pools — a grouping's support can move between gap treatments even where the tree's groupings don't. Compare supports only within one gap treatment.
